a native or inhabitant of Italy
Designed to resemble a handwriting style developed in Italy in the 16th century.
Having letters that slant or lean to the right; oblique.

d.g: A typeface in which the letters slant to the right.
d.x: Names of vessels, as the Kearsarge or the Alabama, are frequently put in italic.

d.g: An oblique handwriting style, such as used by Italian calligraphers of the Renaissance.
d.x: Spenser uses two different scripts: an Elizabethan secretary hand for English texts, and an italic 'mixed' with secretary graphs for Latin texts […]

italic.e: Named after the nation of Italy, as it was first used by an Italian printer, Aldo Manuzio, around 1500. Literally Italy + -ic.

d.g: Characterized by itching. (of a condition)
d.x: an itchy rash

d.g: Feeling an itching sensation; feeling a need to be scratched. (of a person, animal or body part)
d.x: My nose always gets itchy the moment I put on my face mask.

d.g: Causing an itching sensation.
d.x: He refuses to wear the new sweater; he says it’s itchy.

d.g: In a state of agitation; easily alarmed.
d.x: Casy said softly, “All of ’em’s itchy. Them cops been sayin’ how they’re gonna beat the hell outa us an’ run us outa the county. […]”

itchy.e: From Middle English *yicchy, *ȝicchi, from Old English ġiċċiġ (“itchy”), equivalent to itch + -y. Cognate with Scots yeukie (“itchy”), West Frisian jokkerich (“itchy”), Dutch jeukachtig and jeukerig (“itchy”).

d.g: Of a procedure that involves repetition of steps (iteration) to achieve the desired outcome; in computing this may involve a mechanism such as a loop.
Expressive of an action that is repeated with frequency.
A verb showing the iterative aspect.

iterative.e: French itératifbor. English iterative Borrowed from French itératif.

d.g: Habitually travelling from place to place.
d.x: an itinerant preacher or peddler

d.g: One who travels from place to place.
A member of the Travelling Community, whether settled or not.

itinerant.e: From Late Latin itinerantem, present active participle of itineror (“travel”), from itiner-. By surface analysis, Latin itiner- + -ant.

d.g: A distinct physical object.
d.x: Tweezers are great for manipulating small items.

d.g: An object that can be picked up for later use.
A line of text having a legal or other meaning; a separate particular in an account.
d.x: the items in a bill

d.g: A question on a test, which may include its answers.
d.x: The exam has 100 items, each of which includes a correct response and three distractors.

item.e: From Middle English item, from Latin item (“also; in the same manner”). The present English meaning derives from a usage in lists, where the first entry would begin in primis (“firstly”) or imprimis, and the other entries with item (“also, moreover”). Later, the members of lists were referred to as "items".

d.g: The third-person singular neuter personal pronoun used to refer to an inanimate object, abstract entity, or non-human living thing.
d.x: Take this book and put it on the shelf.

d.g: A third-person singular personal pronoun used to refer to a baby or child, especially of unknown gender.
d.x: She took the baby and held it in her arms.

d.g: A third-person singular pronoun used to refer to an unspecified person.
d.x: She had never seen that each human being was different, would react differently, had its own peculiar idiosyncrasies.

d.g: A third-person singular personal pronoun used to refer to an animate referent who is transgender or non-binary.

it.e: From Middle English it, hit ( > dialectal English hit (“it”)), from Old English hit (“it”), from Proto-West Germanic *hit, from Proto-Germanic *hit (“this, this one”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱe (“here; here”). …

d.g: A sensation felt on an area of the skin that causes a person or animal to want to scratch said area.
A constant teasing desire or want.
d.x: ... it left, however, a bee at his ear and an itch to transfer the buzzer's attentions and tease his darling; for she had betrayed herself as right good game.

d.g: To feel itchy; to feel a need to be scratched.
To have a constant, teasing urge; to feel strongly motivated; to want or desire something.
d.x: He started learning to drive and he has been itching for opportunities to practice ever since.

itch.e: From Middle English icche, ȝicche, from Old English ġiċċe (“itch”), from Proto-Germanic *jukjǭ (“itch”), of unknown origin. Cognate with Scots yeuk (“itch, itchiness”), Dutch jeuk (“itch”), German jucken.

d.g: The state of being itchy.

itchiness.e: English itchy Proto-Germanic *-inōną Proto-Indo-European *-dyé- Proto-Germanic *-atjaną Proto-Indo-European *-tus Proto-Germanic *-þuz Proto-Germanic *-assuz Proto-Germanic *-inassuz Proto-West Germanic *-nassī Old English -nes Middle English -nesse English -ness English itchiness From itchy + -ness.

d.g: present participle and gerund of itch
A sensation that itches.
d.x: Itchings, hitherto unknown, are felt all over the body, and render my skin sometimes painfully tender, sometimes quite benumbed, as if it were dead.

itching.e: From Middle English ecchinge, ȝitchinge, ʒicchinde, ʒichande (also unassibilated as yckyng), from Old English ġiċċende (“itching”), from Proto-West Germanic *jukkjandi, present participle of *jukkjan (“to itch”), equivalent to itch + -ing.

d.g: Alternative spelling of itemization.

itemisation.e: English itemise Proto-Indo-European *-tis Proto-Indo-European *-Hō Proto-Indo-European *-tiHō Proto-Italic *-tiō Latin -tiō Latin -ātiōlbor. Old French -ationbor. Middle English -acioun English -ation English itemisation From itemise + -ation.

d.g: The act of making a list of items; an itemizing.
d.x: His itemization of the inventory did seem accurate, however it omitted several crucial entries.

d.g: The system of items available to players and their design and qualities.
d.x: The itemization in this game is terrible. All the good items are so rare, it gives players no desire to grind at all.

itemization.e: Latin itemlbor. Middle English item English item English -ization English itemization From item + -ization.

d.g: A recital or a second performance; a repetition.
A variation or version.
d.x: The architect drafted several iterations of the floorplan before deciding on his final design.

d.g: The use of repetition in a computer program, especially in the form of a loop.
A single repetition of the code within such a repetitive process.
d.x: The code calculates the appropriate value at each iteration.

iteration.e: From Latin iterātiō, from iterō. Morphologically iterate + -ion.

d.g: a college town in central New York on Lake Cayuga

A written schedule of activities for a vacation or road trip.
A route or proposed route of a journey.
An account or record of a journey.
A guidebook for travellers.

itinerary.e: From Middle English itinerarie, from Latin itinerārium (“an account of a journey, a road-book”), from iter (“a way, journey”). By surface analysis, Latin itiner- + -ary.

d.g: A travelling around.

itineration.e: From itinerate + -ion, ultimately borrowed from Medieval Latin itinerātiō, from itineror (“travel”), from itiner-.

d.g: A particular triazole antifungal agent (trademark Sporanox) that may be given orally or intravenously especially to treat blastomycosis and histoplasmosis.

itraconazole.e: Probably from itra- (“alteration of tria(zole)”) + -conazole (“miconazole derivative”).

d.g: Non-Oxford British English standard spelling of italicize.

italicise.e: English italic English -ise English italicise From italic + -ise.

d.g: To put into italics.
To emphasize.

italicize.e: English italic Proto-Indo-European *-id- Proto-Indo-European *-yéti Proto-Indo-European *-idyéti Proto-Hellenic *-íďďō Ancient Greek -ῐ́ζω (-ĭ́zō)bor. Late Latin -izōder. Middle French -iserbor. Middle English -isen English -ize English italicize From italic + -ize.

d.g: Alternative spelling of itemize.

itemise.e: Latin itemlbor. Middle English item English item English -ise English itemise From item + -ise.

d.g: To state in items, or by particulars
d.x: to itemize the cost of a railroad

itemize.e: Latin itemlbor. Middle English item English item Proto-Indo-European *-id- Proto-Indo-European *-yéti Proto-Indo-European *-idyéti Proto-Hellenic *-íďďō Ancient Greek -ῐ́ζω (-ĭ́zō)bor. Late Latin -izōder. Middle French -iserbor. Middle English -isen English -ize English itemize From item + -ize.

d.g: To perform or repeat an action on each item in a set.
d.x: The max() function iterates through the data to find the highest value.

d.g: To perform or repeat an action on the results of each such prior action.
d.x: In mathematics, an iterated function is a function which is composed with itself, possibly ad infinitum, in a process called iteration.

d.g: To repeat an activity, making incremental changes each time.
An n-fold self-composition of a function.

iterate.e: The adjective is first attested in 1471, in Middle English, the verb in 1533, the noun in 1941; partly inherited from Middle English iterat(e) (adjective), partly borrowed from Latin iterātus, perfect passive participle of iterō (“to do something for a second time, repeat”) (see -ate (etymology 1, 2 and 3)) , from iter …

d.g: To travel from place to place, especially to preach or lecture.
